justification:
The major finding that capped round 1 at 6.8 is genuinely fixed, not relabeled. The paragraph in "Telling a client its copy is still good" now reads: ETag supplies a validator: RFC 9110 defines an entity tag as "an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource" ([section 8.8.3]) ... A client that still has a stored response sends that token back in If-None-Match — RFC 9111 describes exactly this: "one or more entity tags, indicating one or more stored responses, can be used in an If-None-Match header field for response validation" ([RFC 9111, section 4.3.1]). I independently fetched both cited sections and both quotations are verbatim matches, each attached to the RFC and section that actually contains it, each used in the context that source actually discusses (8.8.3 for the definition of an entity tag itself; 9111 4.3.1 for how a stored entity tag is used in an If-None-Match validation request). This is a real fix, not a shuffle of the same error to a different citation.

The ETag-truncation caveat reads as honest transparency, not hedging filler: 'Etag below keeps just the first 8 hex characters (32 bits) of the SHA-256 digest so the output stays short enough to read at a glance. That is fine for this demo's three requests, but 32 bits collides far too often for a real deployment; a production implementation should send the full 64-character digest (256 bits)...' It names the specific weakness (collision rate), scopes why the demo's shortcut is acceptable for its own purposes, and gives the production fix in the same breath — exactly the kind of caveat the editorial brief wants instead of a silent simplification.

The collapsed-into-<details> restructuring of 3 of the 5 server programs (families, caching, cookies) does not read as removing substance or padding with filler. Each collapsed block is followed by a `snippet of=` excerpt introduced by a specific sentence naming what's new ('The part of Handle that is new', 'Handle and Etag are what is new here', 'Handle is the only new part'), and in each case the excerpt is in fact the meaningful new logic for that program: the families snippet shows the Expect:100-continue gate plus the status-code-routing switch; the caching snippet shows the ETag computation and the If-None-Match comparison/304 branch; the cookies snippet shows the Set-Cookie/Cookie check logic. The repeated ReadHead/ReadBody/plumbing boilerplate is what's hidden, which is exactly the part a reader has already seen twice by that point in the article. `node tools/run-code.mjs` confirms all five full programs are still present and runnable (blocks=16, up from round 1's 13, consistent with the new snippet-of blocks being additional extracted/checked blocks, not replacements) — nothing was silently dropped from execution.

Run-code: `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/networking/http-explained.md` from PowerShell reports `PASS networking/http-explained.md  blocks=16 executed=6`, matching the writer's claim exactly.

Sanity check on round-1's other strengths: exercise count is still 5 (git diff confirms no exercise was touched), front-matter still lists all 11 sources, and the diff against 5b6bdc7 shows the changes are confined to citation/quote text, the new caveat note, and the details/snippet restructuring — no new demo code was added that would risk new overlap with how-the-internet-works.md (round 1 already confirmed no shared helpers or demos between the two articles, and that boundary is untouched here).

What keeps this below a pass: round 1's AdSense review itself flagged three issues, not one — the major ETag misattribution, a moderate 9.2.1-should-be-9.2.2 citation, and a moderate DELETE-idempotency citation pointing at RFC 9110 section 9.3.5 ('PUT and DELETE add nothing new but are idempotent anyway, each defined that way in its own section ([9.3.4], [9.3.5])'). The writer's round-2 pass fixed the major issue and the 9.2.1→9.2.2 issue (confirmed by diff: the citation on 'Safe methods ... are idempotent by construction' now reads [RFC 9110, section 9.2.2]) but left the DELETE/[9.3.5] citation completely untouched — the diff shows that exact clause unchanged, byte for byte, between round 1 and round 2. I re-fetched RFC 9110 section 9.3.5's full text directly: it describes what a server should do when a DELETE succeeds (status codes, cache invalidation, content-in-DELETE-request guidance) and never uses the word 'idempotent' anywhere in the section, exactly as round 1 found. So the sentence still tells a reader that DELETE's idempotency is 'defined that way in its own section', which is false for DELETE specifically (true for PUT, whose 9.3.4 does say 'the intent of PUT is idempotent'); DELETE's idempotency is established only by the general safe/idempotent list in section 9.2.2. This is a real, previously-identified, independently re-verifiable citation-precision defect that survived a writer pass whose stated purpose was to fix citation precision, which is enough on its own to hold the round back from a pass even though the more serious major-severity fabrication issue is now genuinely resolved.

issues.problem: Unchanged from round 1 and still incorrect for DELETE. RFC 9110 section 9.3.4 (PUT) does state 'the intent of PUT is idempotent', but section 9.3.5 (DELETE), fetched and read in full, never uses the word 'idempotent' anywhere in its text (it covers status codes to return, cache invalidation, and content-in-DELETE-request guidance). DELETE's idempotency comes only from the general safe/idempotent list in section 9.2.2, not from a restatement in DELETE's own section, so citing [9.3.5] for 'defined that way in its own section' misattributes the claim for DELETE specifically. This is the same finding round 1's AdSense review already made; it was not addressed in this round's fixes.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite 9.2.2 for DELETE's idempotency instead of 9.3.5, or rephrase so only PUT is described as restating idempotency in its own section, with DELETE's idempotency attributed to the general list in 9.2.2 (e.g. '`PUT` restates this in its own section ([9.3.4]); `DELETE`'s comes only from the general list above ([9.2.2]).').
